title: Data modelling for NoSQL
subtitle: In DynamoDB and Cassandra you design keys around the questions your app asks. List them first, then shape the data so each one is a single cheap read.

c.v: Discord's 2017 post tells how it moved chat messages from MongoDB to Cassandra. Every query read one channel, so
. Messages inside it were sorted by
The first import showed a problem at once. Cassandra logged warnings about
over 100 MB. Under one key, a busy channel's messages would grow without end. Discord wrote that big partitions add heavy
pressure, and cannot be spread across the cluster.
So they changed the key. They added a time
. They looked at the largest channels and chose about 10 days per bucket. They expected that to keep partitions comfortably under 100 MB.

The model still had a sharp edge. In one public server, someone deleted millions of messages with the API. One message was left in the channel. To return it, Cassandra scanned millions of delete markers, called
The garbage collector ran 10-second stop-the-world pauses again and again.

The fix was in table settings and the read path. Discord cut the tombstone lifetime from 10 days to 2. That was safe only because they ran repairs every night. The query code now remembers empty buckets and skips them.
Nothing here was a bug in Cassandra. The key decided how big each partition could grow, and how much work one read could cause.

AWS says it plainly: you should not design a DynamoDB schema "until you know the questions it will need to answer".
Cassandra's docs say the same: "data modeling is query-driven".
The reason is the trade. These stores answer a few kinds of query very fast at any size. Other queries can be "expensive and slow".
You choose which queries are fast when you choose the keys.
Write the list of access patterns before you draw a table. Then pick a partition key and sort key so each pattern is one request to one partition. Copy data where a pattern needs it.

In DynamoDB you copy into item collections and indexes instead. In the diagram, the club's name is copied onto each membership item. The "my clubs" screen then needs one read, not one per club. The cost is that a club rename must update every copy.

AWS's example is invoices and bills. One Query reads all bills on an invoice. For the reverse, "which invoices contain this bill?", you add a
People call this flipped index an inverted index.
A GSI is not free. It is updated asynchronously, usually "within a fraction of a second". A query on it can return stale results.
Each GSI also adds write cost, and a GSI short of write capacity throttles writes to the table.
A partition key with a few huge values is a trap. In DynamoDB, each partition can serve at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second.
Cassandra suggests under 100,000 values and under 100 MB per partition.
Its hard limit is 2 billion cells, but it gets slow well before that.
The fix is the one Discord used. Add a column to the partition key, such as a month or a date.
Here is the simplified schema from Discord's post. It keeps the newest messages first. The real table has about 10 more columns.

blocks.v:
CREATE TABLE messages (
  channel_id bigint,
  bucket int,
  message_id bigint,
  author_id bigint,
  content text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id, bucket), message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

c.v: The bucket must be computable from the ID or a timestamp.
Reads then walk buckets from now backwards until they have enough rows. The cost lands on quiet channels: they may need several queries to fill one page.
Pick the bucket size from your biggest key, not your average one.
AWS's general advice is to keep "as few tables as possible".
goes further. It stores many entity types in one table, so one Query can return a user and their orders together.
AWS also lists the costs. It has a steep learning curve. All entities share one backup, one encryption setting and one stream.
AWS says multiple tables are "good and sufficient" when you never query entities together.
Alex DeBrie, who recommends it for most apps, gives the main reason: fetching several item types "using a single request".
He lists the downsides too. New
are hard to add, and analytics need extra work. He would skip it for
, and for new apps that value flexibility.
Pete Naylor, who worked at Amazon, pushes back harder. He says: "Do NOT start with exactly one table as a design constraint…"
He agrees the best answer might be one table, but says it often will be more.
Items in one table but different partitions are no cheaper to read than items in two tables.
The real win is the item collection. So treat the number of tables as an outcome of the modelling.

c.v: Here is a worked example: a small sports club app. First, the access patterns. Then the keys. Each row is one request.
Show one court's slots for a day
The bookings query needs an upper bound. A plain
The court partition is bucketed by day, so it holds at most one item per slot. Booking writes two items in one transaction. The condition stops a double booking.

blocks.v:
await ddb.send(new TransactWriteCommand({ TransactItems: [
  { Put: { TableName: "Club",
      Item: { PK: "COURT#c7#2026-11-20", SK: "SLOT#18:00", member: "m1" },
      ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(PK)" } },
  { Put: { TableName: "Club",
      Item: { PK: "MEMBER#m1", SK: "BOOKING#2026-11-20T18:00", court: "c7" } } },
] }));

c.v: Write each access pattern with its key, its sort order and its peak rate. AWS says to know data size, shape and velocity first.
"What is the biggest this partition can get?"
If there is no answer, add a bucket.
For every copied field, name the code that updates it.
"Which question will product ask next year?"
If you can't answer it with a new GSI, say so now.
"Here are our 8 access patterns with rates. Propose a DynamoDB key design. For each pattern, show the exact GetItem or Query call, the PK and SK values, and how many items it reads."
"For this Cassandra schema, estimate the largest partition using our biggest customer's data. Show the formula and the numbers."
"List every field this design copies. For each one, show the code path that must change when the source changes."
Every access pattern maps to one request. None needs a Scan or a filter on a non-key field.
No partition key value can grow without a limit.
The agent did not add a GSI where the base table could already answer.
Code that reads a GSI can handle a missing or stale item.
Transactions stay under 100 items, and the agent counted the double write cost.

q.v: You are starting a new DynamoDB table. What should you write down first?

options.v: The entities and their relationships, fully normalised.
The list of questions the app will ask, with their keys and rates.
The number of tables you want.

why.v: AWS says not to design a DynamoDB schema until you know the questions it must answer. Keys come from those questions.

q.v: A chat table uses channel_id as the only partition key. One busy channel has years of messages. What is the main risk?

options.v: One partition grows without a limit and gets too big and too hot.
The sort order of messages becomes random.
Queries for that channel need a join.

why.v: Everything for one partition key lives together. Discord saw partitions over 100 MB and fixed it by adding a time bucket to the partition key.

q.v: Items have PK = MEMBER#id and SK = CLUB#id. How do you list all members of one club efficiently?

options.v: Scan the table with a filter on SK.
Add a global secondary index whose partition key is the club ID, for example the sort key swapped into the index key.
Use a bigger read capacity on the table.

why.v: The club ID sits in the sort key of many partitions. An inverted index puts all of one club's members in one index partition, so one Query finds them.

q.v: Which statement about DynamoDB transactions is true?

options.v: One transaction can touch any number of items in any Region.
One transaction can touch up to 100 distinct items in one account and Region, and each item costs two writes.
Transactions are free, so you should wrap every write in one.

why.v: TransactWriteItems allows up to 100 distinct items and 4 MB in one account and Region. DynamoDB does a prepare and a commit for each item.

q.v: What is the strongest argument for putting several entity types in one DynamoDB table?

options.v: Fewer tables always make every query faster.
Items that share a partition key can be read together with one Query.
DynamoDB charges per table, not per request.

why.v: The gain comes from the item collection. Items in the same table but different partitions cost the same to read as items in two tables.
